questions.q: A browser receives the PAC file but no proxy-policy log appears when the user opens a site. What should be checked first?
o: Evaluate FindProxyForURL for that exact URL and host.
Increase the isolator server timeout on FortiGate.
Move the explicit proxy policy above firewall policies.
Replace the web-filter profile on the proxy policy.
f: Correct: the PAC function can return DIRECT, so the browser never opens a proxy session.
An isolator timeout matters only after a policy selects isolation and forwards the request.
Proxy-policy order matters after the browser connects to the explicit listener.
A web-filter profile cannot force a browser to use a proxy.

questions.q: Windows rejects an HTTPS PAC download even though the captive-portal URL responds. Which dependency is most likely missing?
o: A matching destination object in the isolator policy.
A custom FortiGate certificate with a trusted CA chain.
A second proxy listener on the WAN interface.
A deep-inspection profile on the PAC download policy.
f: A destination object affects later proxy-policy matching, not PAC TLS validation.
Correct: Windows must trust the custom server certificate and its CA chain.
A second listener does not repair the certificate presented by the PAC service.
Deep inspection is not the prerequisite for the captive-portal HTTPS PAC server.

questions.q: A forward-traffic log shows action isolate, but the user sees a blank isolated browser. What is the next boundary to test?
o: Whether the browser selected DIRECT in its PAC result.
Whether the explicit proxy feature is visible in the GUI.
Whether the configured isolator server is reachable and healthy.
Whether the firewall policy has an SSL inspection profile.
f: A DIRECT result would not produce this proxy-policy isolate log.
Feature visibility is setup state; the isolate log proves the policy path was reached.
Correct: policy selection is proven, but the isolator endpoint and its upstream service are not.
SSL inspection may matter for content inspection, not basic isolator reachability.

questions.q: FortiManager reboots after an executable hash mismatch. Which interpretation best matches RT-FSIC?
o: The self-encrypting drive failed to unlock the administrator database.
A device-install transaction left the ADOM database inconsistent.
The TPM rejected a remote administrator's login certificate.
The runtime integrity control blocked the binary and triggered a reboot.
f: Drive encryption protects stored data; it does not explain a runtime executable hash mismatch.
ADOM install state is separate from the platform executable integrity chain.
TPM-backed boot trust is not the same as a remote administrator login certificate.
Correct: RT-FSIC blocks the untrusted binary and may reboot after mismatch or missing hash.

questions.q: Which control primarily protects data if a FortiManager storage drive is physically removed?
o: Self-encrypting drive protection for data at rest.
UEFI Secure Boot verification of the boot chain.
Trusted-host restrictions on GUI and SSH access.
Runtime hash checks on executable libraries.
f: Correct: drive encryption protects stored data confidentiality if media is removed.
Secure Boot validates the boot chain, not confidentiality of stored records.
Trusted hosts restrict management sources, not offline disk access.
Runtime hash checks protect code integrity, not data-at-rest confidentiality.

questions.q: An engineer can reach the GUI from an unapproved subnet, but boot integrity checks pass. Which control is mis-scoped?
o: TPM support for the hardware trust anchor.
Trusted-host restrictions on management access.
Self-encrypting drive protection for stored data.
Runtime executable hash verification.
f: TPM supports hardware trust; it does not filter GUI source addresses.
Correct: trusted hosts restrict which source addresses may manage the appliance.
Drive encryption has no effect on remote GUI admission.
Runtime integrity verifies binaries, not administrator network origin.

questions.q: A playbook fails at task 3 after task 2 changed its JSON output. What is the most useful 8.0 debugging action?
o: Disable the incident trigger and recreate the playbook.
Increase the FortiAnalyzer log retention period.
Inspect task 2 output and task 3 input, then partially rerun.
Duplicate the connector and bind it to the trigger.
f: Recreating the trigger does not fix a downstream data-contract mismatch.
Retention affects stored logs, not the JSON passed between playbook tasks.
Correct: inspect the exact node boundary, repair the mapping, and restart from the failed node.
A duplicate connector does not establish which output field changed.

questions.q: A connector is visible in the playbook editor but grayed out. What does that indicate?
o: Its API returned a valid payload during the last run.
The trigger has not matched any incidents yet.
The downstream task is waiting for a branch condition.
The connector is inactive or not configured for production use.
f: A previous API response does not prove the connector is currently active.
Trigger matching is separate from connector activation state.
A waiting branch is a task-flow condition, not connector status.
Correct: configure and activate the connector before relying on its action.

questions.q: A dry-run succeeds, but the production playbook cannot create a ticket. Which assumption should be revisited?
o: Mock data validated mapping but did not prove live credentials or permissions.
The Job ID was not retained in the task list.
The Branch node must always be placed before the trigger.
FortiAnalyzer cannot use external connector actions in production.
f: Correct: dry-run validates data flow, not production credentials, API scopes or service availability.
The Job ID helps investigation but does not grant external ticket permissions.
A trigger precedes task execution; Branch placement depends on workflow logic.
External connector actions are the intended production integration model.

questions.q: Only port12 drops unknown multicast while other ports are healthy. Which configuration layer should be inspected first?
o: The global storm-control threshold only.
The port-level storm-control override and effective rate.
The FortiGate firewall policy for multicast traffic.
The LLDP neighbor table for port12.
f: Global settings are the baseline; a port override can change the effective value.
Correct: inspect port12's storm-control-mode and per-port class thresholds.
A FortiGate firewall policy does not explain a local switch ingress drop counter.
LLDP neighbor state is unrelated to the storm-control meter.

questions.q: What does setting storm-control rate to zero mean for an enabled traffic class?
o: The threshold is disabled and all packets pass.
The switch changes from packet rate to byte rate.
All packets of that enabled class are dropped.
The switch falls back to the global default rate.
f: Zero is not a disable value for an enabled class.
The setting remains a packet-rate control; it does not change units.
Correct: the FortiSwitch guide states zero drops all packets for enabled classes.
There is no automatic fallback to a default rate when zero is configured.

questions.q: The storm-control diagnostic shows 140 dropped packets per second. What does this prove?
o: A Layer 2 loop is definitely the root cause.
The switch's STP root has changed.
A specific endpoint generated malicious broadcast traffic.
Storm control is dropping traffic, but the source still needs investigation.
f: A loop is one possible cause, not proven by the drop counter.
The counter does not identify STP root changes.
The counter does not attribute traffic to a malicious endpoint.
Correct: correlate port counters, STP state and captures to find the source.

questions.q: RADIUS returns Tunnel-Private-Group-ID=data, but the client joins the default VLAN. Which configuration is the likely missing link?
o: A matching vlan-name entry and dynamic-vlan enablement on the VAP.
A new captive-portal redirect URL in the Access-Accept.
A second RADIUS accounting server for interim updates.
A different WPA2 cipher suite on the SSID.
f: Correct: the returned name tag must resolve in the VAP's vlan-name table and dynamic VLAN must be enabled.
A redirect URL changes portal navigation, not Layer 2 VLAN resolution.
Accounting redundancy does not determine the VLAN in the Access-Accept.
The cipher suite does not map the RADIUS tag to a VLAN.

questions.q: The wireless client table shows VLAN 200, but the client never receives DHCP. Which boundary is most relevant?
o: Whether the RADIUS server used PEAP or EAP-TLS.
Whether VLAN 200 exists on the bridge/trunk path and has DHCP service.
Whether the RADIUS reply includes a captive-portal URL.
Whether the VAP name-tag pool contains eight VLANs.
f: EAP method may affect authentication but the assigned VLAN is already visible.
Correct: verify VLAN membership on uplinks, the FortiGate interface and its DHCP scope.
A portal URL is not required for DHCP on the assigned VLAN.
Eight entries are only a maximum pool size, not a DHCP requirement.

questions.q: A RADIUS name tag maps to VLANs 100, 200 and 300. Who chooses the actual VLAN for a new authentication?
o: The RADIUS server selects the VLAN ID in a second Access-Accept.
The FortiAP radio chooses based on RSSI.
The wireless controller resolves the tag and allocates from the pool round-robin.
The upstream switch chooses the least-used VLAN.
f: The server returns the logical tag; it does not choose a second VLAN response.
RSSI does not select a VLAN from a name-tag pool.
Correct: FortiGate resolves the VAP mapping and distributes across configured VLAN IDs.
The upstream switch forwards tagged frames; it does not allocate the client VLAN.

questions.q: The FortiNAC primary fails, but the secondary remains in Idle state. What should be examined first?
o: The captive-portal registration expiry timer.
The FortiAP controller's VLAN assignment.
The primary server's web theme configuration.
HA management state and database replication health.
f: Portal expiry does not control HA role election.
Wireless VLAN assignment is downstream of NAC availability.
Web theme settings do not affect the HA management process.
Correct: Idle can mean the secondary is not eligible to take control; inspect HA state and replication.

questions.q: When is a shared IP appropriate for a FortiNAC HA pair?
o: When both appliances are in the same subnet.
When primary and secondary are in different routed subnets.
Only when database replication is disabled.
Only when both nodes share the same hostname.
f: Correct: the 9.4 guide says not to use a shared IP across different subnets.
A routed multi-subnet pair should omit the shared IP and plan access paths.
Database replication is a separate HA function and should remain healthy.
Hostnames do not replace the same-subnet requirement for the shared address.

questions.q: The HA configuration page reports success immediately after Save. What is still required before declaring replication healthy?
o: A new RADIUS shared secret on the secondary.
Verify peer communication and database replication, then complete the service restart sequence.
Disable the shared IP and rely on DNS round-robin.
Force the secondary to become primary before synchronization.
f: RADIUS secrets do not prove database synchronization.
Correct: save initiates peer/replication checks; verify replication and restart services as documented.
DNS round-robin does not provide the shared-IP failover semantics.
Promoting an unsynchronized secondary risks inconsistent state.

questions.q: The outer TEAP TLS tunnel succeeds, but the user identity never appears in the authorization result. What is the strongest next check?
o: The DHCP relay address on the access switch.
The FortiNAC-F endpoint profiler's SNMP community.
The configured primary/secondary inner-authentication order and Windows EAP-TEAP mode.
The FortiSwitch storm-control burst-size level.
f: DHCP relay is unrelated to the inner EAP exchange.
SNMP profiling may enrich host data but does not control TEAP inner method order.
Correct: compare server primary/secondary types with the Windows supplicant's EAP-TEAP mode.
Storm-control burst settings do not affect the RADIUS authentication sequence.

questions.q: FortiNAC-F is configured Primary Computer, Secondary User. Which Windows profile best matches that design?
o: Microsoft EAP-TTLS with PAP and no machine authentication.
PEAP-MSCHAPv2 with user-only authentication.
EAP-TLS with a single machine certificate exchange.
Microsoft EAP-TEAP with the intended user-or-computer authentication mode.
f: TTLS/PAP is a different single-stage method and does not implement the TEAP chain.
User-only PEAP does not provide the required computer-then-user sequence.
Single EAP-TLS machine authentication omits the secondary user stage.
Correct: configure Microsoft EAP-TEAP and align the supplicant mode with server ordering.

questions.q: An Access-Accept is returned, but the design requires both machine and user identity. What evidence is needed?
o: TEAP/RADIUS logs showing both inner authentication stages completed.
Only the switch's link-up event.
Only the outer TLS server certificate expiry date.
A successful DHCP lease from the assigned VLAN.
f: Correct: the final Access-Accept alone does not prove both inner identities were checked.
Link-up proves physical connectivity, not EAP identity stages.
Certificate expiry is one prerequisite, not proof of the inner exchanges.
A DHCP lease is downstream network access evidence, not identity-chain evidence.

questions.q: Why select Proxy as the preferred authentication method for a remote RADIUS server?
o: To convert every EAP exchange into PAP.
To forward the original authentication method and credentials unchanged.
To make FAC perform all user password validation locally.
To bypass the remote RADIUS server and return Access-Accept.
f: Proxy mode does not translate all methods to PAP.
Correct: the remote server receives the original RADIUS authentication method/credentials unchanged.
Local validation is not the purpose of the remote Proxy option.
The remote RADIUS server remains responsible for validating the request.

questions.q: Why enable Include realm in username for a federated RADIUS hierarchy?
o: To remove the suffix before local user lookup.
To force every request to the secondary server.
To preserve the qualified username so downstream proxies can route by realm.
To encrypt the RADIUS shared secret inside the username.
f: The option preserves the realm; it does not strip it.
Secondary server selection is redundancy behavior, not realm routing.
Correct: retaining the realm supports hierarchical proxy routing such as eduroam.
The username is not an encryption container for the shared secret.

questions.q: What changes when Require Message-Authenticator Attribute in Response is enabled?
o: FAC stops including Message-Authenticator in its requests.
FAC converts upstream responses into signed EAP packets.
FAC accepts responses without the attribute but logs a warning.
FAC rejects upstream authentication responses that omit the attribute.
f: FAC always includes the attribute in outgoing authentication requests when it is the RADIUS client.
The setting does not transform RADIUS into EAP or sign EAP packets.
The documented behavior is to accept only responses containing the attribute.
Correct: upstream compatibility is required before enforcing this response check.

questions.q: A Web RDP user authenticates to FortiPAM but lands on the wrong RDS farm host. Which setting is most relevant?
o: The target's Web RDP load-balancing information cookie.
The secret's password rotation schedule.
The target's Windows application filter deny list.
The user's approval tier expiration timer.
f: Correct: the broker cookie tells the connection broker which farm/collection to select.
Password rotation changes credentials, not RDS broker affinity.
Application filters restrict executables and do not choose the RDS host.
Approval expiry controls access authorization, not the broker's host selection.

questions.q: Which prefix is required in the documented Web RDP load-balancing value?
o: https://MS-RDP/ConnectionBroker/
rdp://terminal-services/farm/
tsv://MS Terminal Services
mstsc://broker/loadbalance/
f: This is not the documented Terminal Services cookie prefix.
Correct: Fortinet states the tsv://MS Terminal Services prefix is mandatory.
The prefix is not a generic rdp:// URI.
The broker value does not use an mstsc:// URI.

questions.q: The Loading Balancing Information field is missing from a target. What should be verified?
o: Whether the FortiPAM appliance has a static route to the broker.
Whether the secret uses a password changer.
Whether the target template uses the Web RDP default launcher.
Whether the requester belongs to an ADOM.
f: Routing is needed for reachability but does not control field visibility.
Password changers are unrelated to Web RDP launcher-specific target fields.
Correct: the field is available only for targets using templates with Web RDP default launcher.
ADOMs are FortiManager objects, not FortiPAM target prerequisites.

questions.q: A threat feed contains a 64-character SHA-256 indicator, but the FIM event has a 32-character hash. What is likely?
o: The file was compressed before FortiSIEM parsed it.
The event is a Windows Event Forwarding record.
The hash was truncated by the Collector's hostname mapping.
The agent or event path is still providing an MD5 value.
f: Compression does not explain the algorithm-specific hash length.
WEF transport does not itself convert a FIM hash to a shorter algorithm.
Hostname mapping does not determine file-hash algorithm or length.
Correct: 32 hexadecimal characters typically indicate MD5, while SHA-256 is 64.

questions.q: No FIM event appears after a protected file changes. Which first check is most useful?
o: Verify the monitor template path/change scope, agent health and file permissions.
Increase incident correlation window to 30 minutes.
Change the Windows event parser to a different vendor.
Disable Windows Event Forwarding on the central server.
f: Correct: FIM depends on template scope, agent operation and access to the watched path.
Correlation windows affect incident grouping, not event generation at the endpoint.
Parser changes cannot recover an event the agent never generated.
WEF is separate from native-agent FIM coverage.

questions.q: What does a SHA-256 match to a threat-intelligence indicator establish?
o: The file is definitely executing malicious code.
The file content matches the indicator bytes; context is still needed.
The endpoint is compromised regardless of file location.
The Windows Agent monitor template is complete.
f: A hash match is evidence of content identity, not proof of execution or intent.
Correct: validate source, signer, path, process and activity before containment.
A matching file can be present without execution or compromise.
A hash match does not prove all required paths are monitored.

questions.q: The IPsec tunnel is up, but one Windows application bypasses the Security PoP. What should be checked?
o: The split-DNS suffix list only.
The FortiGate LAN interface MTU first.
The application-based split-tunnel rule and the endpoint profile.
The RADIUS accounting interim-update interval.
f: Split DNS affects name resolution, not the application's packet forwarding decision.
MTU can affect packet delivery but does not explain intentional local bypass classification.
Correct: compare the application's process identity/destination with the endpoint split-tunnel policy.
RADIUS accounting interval does not select local versus tunneled application traffic.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes split DNS from split tunneling?
o: Both features select the same IPsec route for every packet.
Split DNS controls app identity; split tunnel controls certificate trust.
Split DNS chooses firewall policy; split tunnel chooses the DNS resolver.
Split DNS selects name-resolution path; split tunnel selects packet/application forwarding path.
f: They are separate controls and do not share one routing decision.
Certificate trust is part of tunnel authentication, not split DNS.
DNS resolver choice and firewall policy selection are different stages.
Correct: diagnose DNS resolution and packet forwarding as separate transactions.

questions.q: A team wants LDAP authentication for IPsec remote agents. What does the current feature guide say?
o: LDAP authentication is unavailable for IPsec remote agents; use supported SSO, RADIUS or local auth.
LDAP works only when split DNS is disabled.
LDAP is available only on macOS and Linux clients.
LDAP requires an agentless ZTNA bookmark portal.
f: Correct: the guide lists LDAP as unavailable for IPsec remote agents; choose a supported method.
Split DNS does not enable an unsupported authentication method.
The platform limitation is not reversed for macOS/Linux.
Agentless ZTNA is a different access model and does not enable IPsec-agent LDAP.

questions.q: A static route points to an SD-WAN zone, but traffic still fails. Which statement is accurate?
o: The route proves at least one member is healthy.
The zone route resolves logical egress; member health and policy still need verification.
The route bypasses the SD-WAN service rule completely.
The route automatically installs a firewall policy for the zone.
f: A route can exist while every member is down or ineligible.
Correct: verify zone members, service selection and firewall policy separately.
The service rule still determines eligible member/path behavior for matching traffic.
Static routes do not create firewall policy objects.

questions.q: Once interfaces are managed as SD-WAN members, which interface should a firewall policy reference?
o: The physical member name for every WAN link.
The BGP neighbor interface rather than the SD-WAN object.
The logical SD-WAN zone containing the members.
The SLA server address as the outgoing interface.
f: Members are abstracted into zones for policy interface use.
A BGP neighbor is a routing peer, not the policy's logical egress zone.
Correct: policies reference the SD-WAN zone rather than individual member interfaces.
An SLA target is a probe destination, not an interface.

questions.q: Which CLI structure is used for an IPv6 static route referencing an SD-WAN zone?
o: config router bgp with set neighbor-zone
config system sdwan with set route6-member
config router policy with set interface-zone
config router static6 with set sdwan-zone
f: BGP neighbor configuration does not create the IPv6 static route.
The system sdwan table defines members/rules, not the IPv6 route object.
Policy routing is a different routing mechanism.
Correct: IPv6 static routes use config router static6 and set sdwan-zone.

questions.q: After a FortiAnalyzer reboot, device status says Down but new logs are arriving. What is the best interpretation?
o: Device status refresh and log receipt are separate evidence paths.
The playbook trigger is corrupt and must be recreated.
All logs are being rejected by the Analytics database.
The Collector has stopped forwarding logs permanently.
f: Correct: the Community tip reports a 10–15 minute stale status/Last Log display after reboot; verify receipt separately.
A device-status delay does not prove playbook trigger corruption.
Incoming logs contradict a blanket claim that all logs are rejected.
The observed log receipt contradicts a permanent forwarding failure.

questions.q: A PAC script returns PROXY for internal apps but DIRECT for one SaaS hostname. Which layer owns that decision?
o: The FortiGate isolator-server object.
The browser's PAC function evaluation.
The FortiGate firewall policy route table.
The remote RADIUS server's realm mapping.
f: The isolator server is used after a proxy policy selects isolation.
Correct: FindProxyForURL determines PROXY or DIRECT for the requested URL/host.
The routing table is not the component that evaluates PAC JavaScript.
RADIUS realm mapping is unrelated to browser proxy selection.

questions.q: Which pair of controls is most directly responsible for boot trust and runtime executable integrity?
o: Trusted hosts and administrator profiles.
Self-encrypting drives and ADOM workflow sessions.
UEFI Secure Boot and RT-FSIC hash verification.
Policy package checksum and device install preview.
f: Trusted hosts and profiles control management access, not boot/runtime integrity.
Drive encryption protects data at rest; workflow sessions govern configuration changes.
Correct: Secure Boot validates the boot chain; RT-FSIC checks runtime executable integrity.
Policy checksums/install previews do not protect the FortiManager appliance binaries.

questions.q: What is the key protocol difference between the earlier EAP-TTLS/PAP pattern and today's TEAP lesson?
o: TEAP removes the need for an outer TLS tunnel.
TTLS always performs machine authentication before user authentication.
Both methods are equivalent because both use RADIUS.
TEAP can carry sequential inner methods inside a protected outer tunnel.
f: TEAP uses a protected outer tunnel; it does not remove it.
TTLS/PAP does not inherently provide the TEAP machine/user sequence.
Shared RADIUS transport does not make the EAP method mechanics equivalent.
Correct: TEAP's multiple inner methods are the distinct feature taught here.

questions.q: Storm control is dropping broadcast traffic during a loop. What should the engineer do after containment?
o: Identify and correct the loop or faulty endpoint; storm control is not STP.
Disable STP so storm control can learn the topology.
Set rate to zero on every port permanently.
Move the access VLAN to a new subnet.
f: Correct: storm control limits impact; spanning-tree/loop controls and topology repair address the cause.
Disabling STP can worsen the loop and flood.
Zero drops all enabled traffic of that class and is not a repair.
Subnet changes do not remove a Layer 2 loop.

questions.q: How does dynamic VLAN name-tag assignment differ from a RADIUS captive-portal redirect attribute?
o: Both only change the browser's destination URL.
Name tags change the Layer 2 VLAN; redirect attributes change portal navigation.
Redirect attributes determine the DHCP server address.
Name tags select the EAP method after Access-Accept.
f: A name tag changes VLAN resolution, not browser URL navigation.
Correct: one controls the forwarding domain; the other controls where the user is redirected.
DHCP server selection follows VLAN/L3 configuration, not a portal redirect URL.
EAP method negotiation occurs before Access-Accept, not after name-tag processing.

questions.q: Which statement about Message-Authenticator behavior is correct?
o: FAC sends it only when the upstream server requests it.
FAC never validates attributes in upstream responses.
FAC always includes it in outgoing requests and can require it in responses.
It replaces the RADIUS shared secret on both legs.
f: The guide says FAC includes the attribute when acting as the RADIUS client.
Response validation is an optional setting, not universally absent.
Correct: outgoing inclusion is documented; response enforcement is separately configurable.
Message-Authenticator does not replace the shared secret.

questions.q: What does the Web RDP load-balancing cookie control?
o: Which FortiPAM user is allowed to approve the secret.
Which password changer runs before session launch.
Which endpoint agent certificate is presented to the broker.
Which RDS farm/collection host the connection broker selects.
f: Approval roles are controlled by secret access/approval policy, not broker affinity.
Password changers update credentials, not the broker's host selection.
The load-balancing attribute is broker routing metadata, not an endpoint certificate.
Correct: the cookie helps the connection broker select the intended RDS target.

questions.q: Why is native Windows Agent FIM not equivalent to collecting Windows Event Forwarding logs?
o: WEF transports selected Windows event logs; native agent can also provide FIM and other telemetry.
WEF always computes SHA-256 for every file on disk.
FIM only monitors Security event log IDs.
Native agent FIM does not require a monitor template.
f: Correct: WEF covers Windows event logs, while native agent adds FIM/custom logs/Sysmon capabilities.
WEF is not a file integrity scanner and does not hash every file.
FIM monitors configured files/folders, not only Security event IDs.
The agent's monitor template defines change-monitoring scope.

questions.q: Which platform limitation should be considered when deploying application-based split tunnel?
o: All operating systems support the same application rules.
Only Windows FortiClient endpoints support application-based split tunnel; other platforms use full tunnel.
Linux supports application-based split tunnel but Windows does not.
The feature requires agentless ZTNA and a browser portal.
f: The guide explicitly distinguishes Windows from other endpoint platforms.
Correct: Windows supports application-based split or full tunnel; other platforms support full tunnel only.
This reverses the documented platform support.
Agentless ZTNA is a separate browser-based private-access feature.

questions.q: What is the relationship between a static route using a zone and an SD-WAN service rule?
o: The service rule installs the static route automatically.
The route chooses a physical member; the rule only changes DNS.
The route resolves a logical zone; the service rule selects an eligible member.
The firewall policy replaces both route lookup and member selection.
f: A service rule does not automatically create the static route.
The route references a zone, not a fixed physical member; DNS is separate.
Correct: routing chooses the logical egress zone, then SD-WAN selects an eligible member.
Firewall policy permits traffic; it does not replace routing or SD-WAN selection.

questions.q: After FortiNAC HA failover, the shared IP moved but Persistent Agents cannot reconnect. What should be checked?
o: Only the primary database's schema version.
The FortiGate SD-WAN BGP community.
The FortiAP RADIUS VLAN name tag.
Secondary service state, agent path and Control/Application Server pairing.
f: Database schema is not the only service/agent reachability dependency.
BGP community is unrelated unless routing to the NAC subnet is specifically implicated.
Wireless VLAN mapping does not explain agent reconnect after NAC failover.
Correct: shared-IP movement does not prove services and agent communication recovered.

questions.q: RADIUS Access-Accept is correct and the VAP maps the name tag to VLAN 200. Which test best proves end-to-end forwarding?
o: Verify the VLAN is allowed on the uplink and inspect DHCP/gateway traffic.
Confirm the client received an EAP Success message only.
Check the captive-portal redirect URL on the RADIUS server.
Increase the RADIUS timeout from three to ten seconds.
f: Correct: VLAN trunk membership plus DHCP/gateway packets prove the post-authentication data path.
EAP Success proves authentication, not VLAN reachability or DHCP.
A redirect URL is unrelated to the VLAN's Layer 2 path.
A longer RADIUS timeout does not fix missing VLAN transport.

questions.q: A production connector action fails although node JSON mapping is correct. Which evidence should be examined next?
o: The FortiSwitch port's storm-control counter.
The connector's active state, credentials, scopes and external API response.
The FortiGate PAC function for the destination URL.
The FortiNAC HA shared-IP ownership.
f: Switch counters do not establish external API authorization.
Correct: a valid payload can still fail due to inactive connector, expired credentials or insufficient API scope.
PAC selection is unrelated to FortiAnalyzer connector execution.
NAC shared-IP state is a separate product's HA mechanism.
